title: Distributed transactions: reaching one decision
lead: Machines participating in one transaction must agree on its outcome, even when messages are delayed and processes restart.
goals: Detect global deadlock by combining local graphs
Simulate prepare, vote, decision, and acknowledgement
Explain why a prepared participant can become blocked

sections.title: Two global problems
sections.html:
Locks can be managed where their data resides. However, acyclic local waits-for graphs do not prove that the entire system is deadlock-free: combining their edges may reveal a cycle. Commit also requires a common decision rather than independent choices by each machine.

For example, N1 sees T1 → T2, N2 sees T2 → T3, and N3 sees T3 → T1. Each node sees just one edge, but their union is cyclic. Detecting this requires global information or an equivalent distributed detection protocol.

Data placement and global dependency graphs

In the lecture’s partitioned shared-nothing model, each machine owns its CPU, RAM and local storage, and holds a different portion of the data. This placement model does not by itself create replicas. A coordinator orchestrates the transaction, while participants manage relevant local data and locks. A coarse lock on a whole table also needs an authority that covers that logical table across partitions; independently granting local fragments is not a global table lock.

A two-node version is enough for the same failure: N1 sees T1→T2, while N2 sees T2→T1. Each edge describes current waiting, not an already executed read/write conflict. Combining them gives a global waiting cycle.

Can acyclic local waits-for graphs establish global deadlock freedom?

Worked answer. No. The union can contain a cycle assembled from edges on different nodes.

Do acyclic local waits-for graphs prove global deadlock freedom?

Worked answer. No. Edges on different nodes can combine into a cycle. Two nodes with T1→T2 and T2→T1 already provide a counterexample.

sections.title: Worked example: moving stock between regions
sections.html:
East subtracts 4 crates while West adds 4. If East commits and West aborts, the total is incorrect. Coordinator C must therefore establish one decision for participants E/W.

  1. Prepare: C asks whether E/W are ready to commit.
  2. Vote: each participant checks its conditions. To vote YES, it first durably records PREPARE and the necessary recovery information. Otherwise, it votes NO.
  3. Decide: C may choose COMMIT only after receiving every YES; one NO requires ABORT. C durably records its decision before announcing it.
  4. Finish: E/W record and implement the final decision, then send ACK (an acknowledgement).

E might vote NO because it lacks enough stock. Once E promises YES, it must be able to follow the final decision even after restarting. This is why its PREPARE log must be durable before the vote is sent.

Key takeaway

2PC coordinates commit; 2PL controls concurrent reads and writes. Two-phase commit protects atomic commit across machines. It does not replace an isolation protocol such as two-phase locking.

Both names contain “two-phase,” but the phases have different meanings: prepare/decision in 2PC, and growing/shrinking lock phases in 2PL.

Durable decisions precede their protocol messages

The phase trace has three durable-before-message boundaries: participant PREPARE before YES; coordinator COMMIT before announcing COMMIT; and, under the stated protocol, participant COMMIT before ACK. A crash after one of those messages must leave enough log evidence to honor it. Applying the decision still requires the participant’s local recovery actions.

Once COMMIT is durable, a missing ACK does not reopen the vote or allow the coordinator to choose ABORT. It resends the decision and collects acknowledgements according to participant state. END records completion/bookkeeping rather than a new commit decision. The forcing of END depends on the detailed protocol/optimization variant; do not infer one universal force rule from differently annotated slide diagrams.

The coordinator recorded COMMIT, then lost one participant ACK. May it switch to ABORT?

Worked answer. No. The decision is already fixed. It must recover/resend that decision and handle repeated acknowledgements without applying the stock change twice.

The coordinator has durable COMMIT but one ACK is missing. May it choose ABORT instead?

Worked answer. No. The outcome is fixed and may already have been applied elsewhere. Resend COMMIT and handle acknowledgements according to participant state, without applying the four-crate change twice.

sections.title: Crash checklist: which log records matter?
sections.html:
Consider four failure points in the example:

  • E loses contact before preparing: it may abort locally.
  • E has logged PREPARE and sent YES: it cannot change its mind merely because of a timeout.
  • C has logged COMMIT but not yet sent it to W: after recovery, C resends the decision.
  • W has committed but its ACK is lost: W sends ACK again without subtracting or adding the stock a second time.

Repeated messages must be handled according to transaction state. Sequence numbers and transaction IDs distinguish retransmissions from new work.

Recovery tables require a protocol convention

In the lecture's presumed-abort variant, a recovering coordinator with COMMIT but no END repeats phase 2; COMMIT with END is finished. ABORT requires no further commit-protocol work in the stated optimized convention. If the coordinator has no transaction entry, presumed abort lets it answer ABORT. That absence rule belongs to this variant; it is not a universal consequence of every atomic-commit log design.

A participant with no PREPARE can abort locally. A prepared participant with a recorded COMMIT can complete/acknowledge it; one with PREPARE alone must ask for the outcome or wait. A recorded ABORT can finish without additional protocol work under the stated variant, but “no protocol work” does not mean its local undo/cleanup obligations disappear.

These recovery cases leave PREPARE alone unresolved. The next section explains why its two possible remote states prevent a safe local timeout decision.

In presumed abort, why is a coordinator's missing entry different from a participant's durable PREPARE?

Worked answer. The coordinator's absence rule is part of the specified presumed-abort protocol. A prepared participant has already promised to obey the final decision and must resolve it; local absence of COMMIT is insufficient.

Message ordering, lock retention and in-doubt recovery

Number messages consecutively within a declared stream, such as one sender/receiver pair for one transaction. “Dense” means each expected next number is the previous number plus one. If message k is missing and k+1 arrives for that stream, the receiver can buffer k+1 until the predecessor is resolved. Numbering detects gaps/retransmissions; it does not guarantee delivery, and a number from a different stream does not fill the gap.

Under the lecture's strict locking convention, both S and X locks are retained until transaction completion, including the prepared/in-doubt interval. Do not undo a durable prepared participant as an ordinary single-node loser before obtaining its permitted global outcome. This connects isolation, recovery and atomic commit: releasing locks or locally rolling back can expose an outcome inconsistent with an already committed remote participant.

A prepared participant times out and releases its X lock so readers can continue. Is that justified?

Worked answer. No. Timeout has not established ABORT, and another participant may already have committed. The decision and recovery protocol must resolve the in-doubt state before completion/release.

Why is a missing coordinator entry different from a participant having durable PREPARE?

Worked answer. The coordinator absence rule belongs to the stated presumed-abort variant. A prepared participant has promised to obey the shared decision; absence of local COMMIT does not show that another node has not committed.

sections.title: Why can a prepared participant not simply abort?
sections.html:
E sees only PREPARE in its log. It cannot yet distinguish two situations: C has not decided, or C has already committed and W has applied the decision. If E independently aborts in the second situation, the regions disagree permanently. To preserve atomicity, E must obtain the decision from C or a participant that knows it. If sufficiently reliable information is unavailable, E must wait.

Key takeaway

A timeout does not prove that the transaction aborted. Another machine may already have committed while its notification was lost. A prepared participant cannot independently abort merely to stop waiting.

If E holds locks, this wait also blocks other transactions. A protocol can therefore preserve atomicity while reducing availability. A timeout means only that information has not arrived in time; it does not establish that the other party has not committed.

Does a YES vote let a participant commit independently when the coordinator becomes unreachable?

Worked answer. No. YES promises readiness, but another participant may have voted NO. Independent abort is also unsafe if another node has committed. The participant needs the permitted shared outcome, rather than a timeout alone.

sections.title: Exercise: combining 2PL and 2PC
sections.html:
T1 has updated stock at E/W and entered PREPARE. T2 wants to read the same item at E. Under strict 2PL, T2 must still wait for T1's final decision. Draw two timelines: one for lock retention and one for commit messages. They meet at transaction completion.

Check your understanding: why does adding replicas not by itself prove that the protocol is nonblocking? You must also specify which replica has authority to decide and how that decision is recorded or agreed upon. Protocols such as Paxos Commit are mentioned as extensions, without a full treatment in this lecture.

Optional extension: consensus is not a majority of participant votes

Beyond the core lecture, Paxos Commit uses replicated agreement to record participant outcomes with a different failure/progress design. Decision-replica quorums and transaction-participant readiness are different sets and serve different purposes. A majority of replicas knowing East voted YES cannot authorize committing a transaction for which West voted NO.

Basic 2PC may block a prepared participant that cannot obtain the decision. This is not the claim that every single failure makes all work unavailable. Replication by itself also does not prove nonblocking behavior: authority, durable agreement, failure assumptions and communication conditions must be specified.

Original distinction: East and West are transaction participants; three other nodes replicate decision information. Two decision replicas can form a quorum, but West's NO still prevents COMMIT for the transaction. Read a protocol's safety and progress assumptions separately instead of replacing “all participants ready” with “a majority says ready.”

Does a decision-replica majority allow ignoring a transaction participant's NO vote?

Worked answer. No. Replica agreement records the required outcome; it does not remove the atomic-commit condition that every participant must be able to commit.

T1 has prepared at E/W. May T2 read the stock at E immediately?

Worked answer. Not if the access conflicts with a lock retained by T1. PREPARE is a promise awaiting the decision, not completion. Strict 2PL releases access after T1 resolves and completes under the protocol.

quiz.question: A participant has only a durable PREPARE record and loses contact with the coordinator. What is safe?
options: Commit independently because it voted YES
Abort immediately when a timeout expires
Seek the decision; it may have to wait
Delete the log and start over
quiz.explanation: A YES vote is a promise to follow the common decision. The coordinator may already have committed elsewhere.

source.summary: Lecture 22 studies partitioned, nonreplicated data, distributed locking, global deadlock, two-phase commit, and the coordination of logging with recovery. Two-phase commit can block progress when the coordinator is unreachable.

limitations: The lecture assumes partitioning without replication. Consensus-based improvements are mentioned but not developed in detail.
